You understand spoken, colloquial Italian (dislocations, “mica”, “tipo”, “boh”, “un sacco”), youth slang (figo, beccare, sgamare) and Florentine (babbo, ganzo, mi garba, icché), and you know when to use them and when not to.
to catch, to hit on / to catch out
at all, not exactly (strengthens a negative)
no problem! / you must be joking!
the child / the little girl (in Tuscany)
the Tuscan aspiration of consonants (la hasa)
Are you having the coffee or not?
It’s not easy at all, you know.
There were loads of people, like three hundred.
What are you saying? We’re going to the seaside tomorrow.
This bread is unsalted: it needs salt.
To recognise features of spoken Italian: dislocation (Il caffè lo prendi?), all-purpose “che”, “c’ho”, “ci” with “avere”.
To understand fillers and interjections: tipo, cioè, boh, dai, figurati, insomma, mica.
To understand youth slang: figo, sfigato, beccare, sgamare, fregare, un casino, un sacco.
To recognise Florentine: babbo, bimbo, ganzo, mi garba, icché, “noi si va”, the Tuscan gorgia.
To choose the right register: with friends, at school, in a formal letter.
To “translate” a colloquial sentence into standard Italian and back.
Florence, November. For the youth page of Mancini’s newspaper, Pietro and Bianca record how people in the neighbourhood speak. The first is Guido, the former cobbler, a Florentine born and bred.
Signor Guido, do you mind if we record? It’s for the newspaper.
No problem, little one. What do you want to know?
How people spoke in Florence when you were young.
Like now, but better. My dad used to say: “We go to the workshop at seven, and whoever’s late skips breakfast.”
And how should you say it? La hasa, la hoha hola. We swallow the C. It’s the gorgia, little one. It’s cool.
And young people today? Do you like how they talk?
Not much. They say “tipo” every three words. Tipo here, tipo there. But tipo what?
Dunno. Then it’s catching. Switch that gadget off, come on, we’re going for a coffee.
In Florence, C between vowels becomes an aspirated H: la hasa, la hoha hola.
T and P soften between vowels too: “la thorta”, “il phapa” — weaker than C.
C’ho fame. Ce l’hai la penna?
Gli ho detto (a lei) di venire.
These forms are normal in speech, even among educated people. But in an essay, a formal letter or an exam, use the standard form: “ho fame”, not “c’ho fame”; “penso che sia”, not “penso che è”.
Cioè, non è che non mi piaccia…
Dai, vieni! — Dai, non ci credo!
no problem / you must be joking
“Mica” strengthens a negative: “Non è mica facile” = It’s not easy at all. On its own, at the start: “Mica male!” = Not bad at all! “Mica vorrai partire?” = You’re not thinking of leaving, are you?
to catch, to hit on; to meet up
“Un sacco” is used by everyone: “Ti voglio un sacco di bene” = I love you loads. “Casino” is informal (careful: originally it means “brothel”); avoid it in formal situations.
il bambino / la bambina; il ragazzo
the child; the boy / the girl
“Noi si va, noi si mangia”: Florentines use “si” + third person instead of “noi andiamo”. Traditional Tuscan bread is “sciocco”, that is, without salt.
Ce l’hai la penna? Me la presti?
Hai una penna? Me la presteresti?
Scusi, avrebbe una penna da prestarmi?
Speaking well doesn’t mean always speaking formally. It means choosing the right register for the right person and situation, like the right clothes for the occasion.
— Where’s Pietro? — Dunno, I don’t know.
What is the standard version of “C’ho fame”?
In an e-mail to the head teacher you write:
Perché Pietro e Bianca intervistano Guido?
Che cosa non piace a Guido dei giovani?
Che cosa scopre Bianca alla fine?

It was Mancini who had the idea, as always. In mid-November, after the success of Pietro’s story at San Frediano, the Gazzetta dell’Oltrarno decided to devote its youth page, “Sotto i vent’anni”, to a new topic: how people speak in Florence. Not the Italian of books, said Mancini, but the real one, the Italian of the streets, the bars, the kitchens, the buses. The one you hear but don’t write down. He entrusted the investigation to Pietro and Bianca, with a twenty-year-old digital recorder and a single piece of advice: “Listen to everyone, judge no one.” Bianca was over the moon. It was exactly the kind of work she dreamed of doing at university: going around with a recorder collecting people’s words, like a botanist collecting plants before they disappear. Pietro was a little less enthusiastic. He was afraid of looking ridiculous, stopping people in the street. Bianca told him linguists had always been a little ridiculous, and that it was the price to pay. They made a list of ten people to interview. The first name on the list was Guido.

Guido was seventy-five, had been born in via Toscanella and had never left the Oltrarno, except once, for military service in Udine, which he still talked about like exile in Siberia. Since reopening his cobbler’s shop in via Maggio two years earlier, he spent his days sitting at his bench in front of the window, hammer in hand and a shoe on his knees, commenting on everything that went by in the street. He spoke a broad, pure Florentine that was heard less and less in Florence. He aspirated his Cs as if he had a river in his throat: “la hasa”, “la hoha hola hon la hannuccia”, “gli amihi”. He said “babbo” instead of “papà”, “bimbo” instead of “ragazzo”, “icché” instead of “che cosa”, and used a construction Bianca found marvellous: “Noi si va”, “noi si mangia”, “noi si dice”, instead of “noi andiamo”, “noi mangiamo”, “noi diciamo”. When Bianca asked whether they could record him, Guido replied “figurati, bimba”, adjusted his cap, cleared his throat and began to speak like an actor who had been waiting for that moment all his life.

The interview lasted two and a half hours. Guido talked about his father, who had been a cobbler before him and who opened the shop at seven sharp, and whoever came late “skipped breakfast”. He talked about the nicknames people gave each other in via Toscanella, where nobody went by their own name: there was the Cricket, the Mouse, Pretty Boy, the Shin, Gina from the Haberdashery. He talked about the words his mother used that nobody used any more: “gnamo”, for “let’s go”; “diaccio”, for “frozen”; “bischero”, for “silly”, but affectionately, the way you say it to a friend; “grullo”, “ciuco”, “trogolo”. Bianca took notes like a woman possessed, and every now and then interrupted him to ask him to repeat a word, explain it, say where it came from. Pietro, next to her, listened and thought of Graziella. His grandmother said some of those words too, but less and less, and almost only when she was angry or tired. He thought Florentine was like the mud of 1966: something that had once been everywhere, and that now had to be searched for carefully, in corners, to find a little more of it.

At the end of the interview, Bianca asked Guido what he thought of the way young people talk today. Guido snorted. He said young people talked badly. That they said “tipo” every three words, “tipo here, tipo there, tipo dunno”, and he never understood tipo what. That they said “cioè” at the start of every sentence, even when there was nothing to explain. That they said “figo” about everything, a shoe, a film, a girl, a sandwich, and that by calling everything figo, nothing was figo any more. That they mixed English into Italian like water into wine: “il meeting”, “lo shopping”, “il weekend”, “fare un post”. “In my day,” he concluded, “people spoke better.” Bianca, who had the recorder on, pointed out very kindly that in the previous two hours he had said “tipo” eleven times. Guido looked at her in disbelief. Then he burst out laughing so hard that he had to lean on his bench. “Dunno,” he said. “Then it’s catching. Switch that gadget off, come on, we’re going for a coffee.”

The second interview was Davide, and it was the opposite of the first. Davide had just turned sixteen and spoke the way all the kids at his school spoke, an art high school full of people from all over the city and half the province. Pietro and Bianca recorded him one evening at the bar below the workshop, while he told them about his week. In ten minutes Davide said “tipo” twenty-three times, “cioè” fifteen times, “raga” eight times, and used a whole lot of words Bianca had never heard or knew with a different meaning. He said a teacher had “sgamato” him while he was drawing in the maths lesson. He said the new project at the Uffizi was “una bomba”, that the museum room had been “pienissima, un casino di gente”, and that he was “in fissa” with a Flemish painter. He said a classmate who never studied “se la tirava” and that another one “era fuori come un balcone”. He said the history test had gone “da schifo”, but that the teacher “non lo beccava mai” anyway. Then, noticing they were staring at him open-mouthed, he stopped. “What?” he asked. “Did I say something weird?”

Bianca asked him to translate. Davide laughed, but agreed, and for half an hour he acted as interpreter of his own language, with the seriousness of a professor. “Sgamare” meant catching someone doing something in secret. “Una bomba” meant something wonderful, fantastic, not something that explodes. “Un casino di gente” meant loads and loads of people. “Essere in fissa” with something meant being obsessed with it. “Tirarsela” meant putting on airs. “Essere fuori come un balcone” meant being a bit crazy. “Da schifo” meant terribly. “Beccare” meant lots of things: to take, to discover, to meet, to guess. “Ci becchiamo dopo” meant see you later. Bianca wrote it all down, in a column next to Guido’s words. At the end she looked at the two columns side by side and said something Pietro found brilliant. “Guido and Davide live three hundred metres apart,” she said. “They both speak Italian. And to understand each other they’d need a translator.” Davide shrugged. “As if,” he said. “Guido resoled my shoes last week. We understand each other perfectly.”

That evening Bianca took Pietro to Bellini’s workshop, where the old dictionary in which they had looked up “abbraccioso” still was. It was a 1950 edition, with a worn green cloth cover. Bianca opened it at the letter G and looked up “ganzo”. It was there. But next to the word, in brackets, it said: “vulg.”, that is, vulgar. “See?” said Bianca. “Seventy-nine years ago, ‘ganzo’ was a rude word. Street kids said it, and teachers told them off. Now Guido says it, at seventy-five, and it seems to us an old, likeable word that needs protecting.” Then she looked up “figo”, and didn’t find it: in 1950 it didn’t exist yet. Pietro understood where she was going. Davide’s slang, which seemed to Guido the ruin of the language, was exactly what Guido’s Florentine had been seventy years before. “In fifty years,” said Bianca, “some linguist will record Davide as an old man, with his old words. ‘Sgamare’, ‘in fissa’, ‘una bomba’. And the young people then won’t understand them.” Pietro laughed at the thought of an old Davide, sitting in front of a shop, complaining that young people don’t talk the way they used to.

The third interviewee was Karl, and it was an unintentionally comic interview. Since becoming a partner in the trattoria, Karl had decided he had to learn Florentine as well as Italian, because a partner, he said, must speak the customers’ language. The problem was that he was learning it from Guido, in the ten-minute break he took every afternoon for a coffee at the counter, and he applied it with the enthusiasm and precision of an engineer, that is, with no sense of proportion. That week he had greeted an American couple with “Bimbi, icché vu’ mangiate?”, and the tourists, who were sixty, had exchanged worried looks. He had told Graziella that the ribollita of the day was “ganzissima”, and Graziella had answered that ribollita was neither ganza nor sciocca, it was ribollita. And above all he had tried to aspirate his Cs, with disastrous results: when he said “la hasa” he sounded as if he were choking, and when he said “la hoha hola” Viola laughed so hard she had to leave the kitchen. During the interview Karl explained that he wanted to fit in. Bianca pointed out to him, very gently, that no Florentine under sixty talked like that any more.

Karl was hurt. He didn’t say so, but Pietro understood from the way he took off his apron and folded it, slowly, with exaggerated care. It was Graziella, that evening, who put things right. She called him into the kitchen after closing, poured him a glass of wine and told him something that Pietro, drying glasses on the other side of the counter, secretly overheard. She told him Florentine isn’t learned like a language, but like a recipe: you don’t put in all the ingredients at once, you add one at a time, a little, and taste. “One word now and then,” she said. “At the right moment. With the right person. If you say ‘babbo’ to a tourist, you’re ridiculous. If you say it to Viola when she asks where Matei is, you’re one of us.” Karl thought about it for a long time. Then he asked what the first word to learn should be. Graziella smiled. “Bischero,” she said. “But you can only say it to friends. And only with a smile.” The next day Karl used it for the first time, with Guido, who had played a trick on him with the salt. Guido laughed so much he gave him a new pair of shoelaces.

Giulia too, when she read the transcripts, told a story Pietro didn’t know. When she had come to Florence at twenty to study restoration, she spoke with a strong Neapolitan accent, with open vowels and the words of the gulf. Her fellow students teased her, not maliciously, but with that slightly unpleasant superiority Florentines sometimes have towards people from the south. They called her “la terrona”, and imitated the way she said “guaglione” and “uè”. So in a year Giulia had learned to hide her accent. She had listened to the radio, repeated words in front of the mirror, corrected every vowel. Now she spoke a neutral, clean Italian, like a newsreader. “But when I go back to Sorrento,” she said, “after a day the accent comes back. Like water finding its bed again.” Matei asked her why she had never told him. Giulia shrugged. “I was ashamed,” she said. “Not any more. Now I’m sorry I hid it. It was something of mine.” Viola, listening from the sofa, said only: “Uè, mammà!” Giulia laughed until she cried.

The interviews went on all week. They recorded the fruit seller in piazza Santo Spirito, who spoke a Florentine as fast as a machine gun and called every customer “tesoro”, even the traffic wardens. They recorded a tour guide who in ten minutes switched from Italian to English to French without noticing, and said “il Ponte Vecchio” in a different tone depending on the group’s language. They recorded two little girls from Viola’s school, playing hide-and-seek in the playground and speaking an Italian full of English words from video games: “Sei out!”, “Hai skippato!”, “Respawna!”. They recorded a Neapolitan taxi driver who had lived in Florence for thirty years and spoke a language all his own, half Neapolitan and half Florentine, with aspirated Cs and open vowels, which Bianca enthusiastically called “il fiorentano”. And they recorded Ion, on the phone from Sibiu, who spoke an Italian learned on trains in the nineties, with words nobody in Italy had used for decades, like “la ferrovia” for the train and “il rapido” for high-speed trains. Every evening, at home, Bianca transcribed the recordings in a new green notebook she had titled: “Firenze parla”.

One evening Andrei video-called from Sibiu, and Bianca, who never missed an opportunity, interviewed him about Romanian youth slang. Andrei had great fun. He explained that in Romanian, to say “figo”, you said “mișto”, a word that came from the Romani language and that everyone used, from children to grandparents. That to say “sfigato” you said “nasol”. That boys in Sibiu called all their friends “frate”, brother, the way boys in Florence said “raga” or “bro”. And that in Romania too grandparents complained that young people put English everywhere. Bianca took notes in a new column of the green notebook, titled “Sibiu”. At one point Andrei asked her how you said “ti voglio bene” in Florentine. Bianca blushed. Pietro, sitting next to her, pretended to look for something in his backpack. Bianca said you said it as in Italian, but with the gorgia: “ti voglio bene” had no C, so it didn’t change. Andrei laughed and said that in that case it was a sentence that worked in both languages. Bianca ended the call rather quickly, and for the rest of the evening she transcribed in silence.

It was during that week that Pietro had a problem at school. His Italian teacher, Professor Orlandi, a strict and passionate woman who quoted Dante from memory and had never given a ten in her life, handed back the essays on “the ideal city”. Pietro got six and a half. It was the lowest mark he had ever got in Italian. Under the essay, in red, the teacher had written: “Excellent ideas, wrong register.” And she had underlined a series of expressions: “c’ho pensato un sacco”, “la gente non è mica scema”, “tipo i parchi”, “un casino di macchine”, “il sindaco gli ho scritto”. Pietro was stunned. He hadn’t noticed. After a week spent listening to spoken language, loving it, transcribing it, the spoken language had slipped into his pen without asking permission. At the end of the lesson he went to see the teacher. She explained that spoken language wasn’t wrong: it was wrong there. “Your essay,” she said, “is like turning up at a wedding in a tracksuit. A tracksuit is perfectly fine for running. But not for a wedding.”

Davide, when he heard about the six and a half, showed no mercy. “You’re a loser,” he said, laughing, at the bar below the workshop. “The king of words, caught out by Orlandi.” Pietro answered that it was easy for him to talk, since at school he got seven in Italian only because he drew nicely in the margins. Davide stopped laughing. He took a sheet folded in four out of his backpack and handed it to him. It was the text of the audio description for the second touchable reproduction at the Uffizi, Leonardo’s Annunciation, which Davide had written on his own, without Pietro’s help. Pietro read it. It was written in perfect, elegant, precise Italian, without a single “tipo”, without a single “cioè”. “The light enters from the left and settles on the face of the Virgin, who raises her right hand in a gesture of restrained surprise.” Pietro looked up, astonished. Davide shrugged. “I’ve got my good suit too,” he said. “I just don’t wear it to the bar.” Pietro gave him back the sheet. For the first time he understood that Davide’s slang wasn’t a poor language. It was an extra language.

Pietro came home downhearted and talked about it at dinner. He expected his grandmother to take his side, since she had been speaking Florentine for seventy-five years. Instead Graziella sided with the teacher. She said that she too, in the trattoria, spoke in three different ways, depending on who was in front of her. With Guido and the fruit seller she spoke broad Florentine, with aspirated Cs and “bischero”. With customers she spoke a kind, clean Italian: “good evening, have a seat, what can I bring you”. And with important people, the mayor, the bishop, the notary, she spoke an Italian so elegant that Pietro had never heard her use it. “It’s called good manners,” she said. “It isn’t being fake. It’s respecting the person in front of you.” Then she told him that once, many years before, the president of the Region had come to the trattoria, and Aldo, who was nervous, had said to him “Icché gli porto, presidente?”. The president had burst out laughing, and from that day he became a regular. “But,” Graziella added, “Aldo could get away with it. He was charming. In an essay you can’t be charming. In an essay you have to be good.”

That evening Pietro rewrote the essay from scratch, for himself, without having to hand it in. It was a strange exercise: taking each sentence and translating it from Italian into Italian, the way Davide had translated his language for Bianca. “C’ho pensato un sacco” became “ci ho riflettuto a lungo”. “La gente non è mica scema” became “i cittadini non sono affatto ingenui”. “Tipo i parchi” became “come, ad esempio, i parchi”. “Un casino di macchine” became “un traffico intensissimo”. “Il sindaco gli ho scritto” became “ho scritto al sindaco”. In the end the essay was longer, colder, and undoubtedly more correct. Pietro reread it and felt something was missing. Then he understood what. His voice was missing. The right essay was correct, but it was no longer his. The wrong essay was incorrect, but it was alive. He talked about it the next day with Bianca, who thought for a long time. Then she said that perhaps skill wasn’t in choosing between the two languages, but in knowing how to use both. “Like Calvino,” she said. “He wrote perfect Italian. But every now and then he put in one street word, just one, and the sentence came alive.”

The twist came at the end of the week, from where nobody expected it: from Viola. Bianca wanted to record her too, to have the voice of the little ones, and interviewed her in the kitchen, sitting on the stool with Assunta’s thimble on her thumb. She asked her what she liked doing. Viola answered with a sentence that made Bianca drop her pen. “Mi garba un sacco disegnare con Davide,” she said, “perché lui è ganzo e mi fa vedere i quadri con le mani. Ma il babbo dice che prima si fanno i compiti.” Pietro and Bianca looked at each other. In a single sentence, a six-year-old girl, the daughter of a Romanian and a woman from Sorrento, had used three words of broad Florentine that none of her classmates knew: “garba”, “ganzo”, “babbo”. Plus “un sacco”, which was young people’s Italian, and “si fanno”, which was pure Florentine. Bianca asked her where she had learned them. Viola shrugged, as if the question were silly. “From Nonna Graziella,” she said. “And from Guido. They talk like that. It’s the language of home.”

Matei, when he heard, was more struck than anyone. That evening, putting Viola to bed, he asked her whether she knew that “babbo” was a Florentine word, that in Sibiu he called his father “tata”, and that her mother, in Sorrento, called her father “papà”. Viola thought about it, with the seriousness she kept for important things. Then she said that in that case she had three dads: babbo in Florence, tata in Sibiu and papà in Sorrento. And that all three were him. Matei laughed, but then, when he left the room, he stopped in the corridor in front of the door frame with the notches and stayed there for a long time. Giulia found him like that. He told her that when he had come to Florence, many years before, he had been afraid that his children, if he had any, would lose Romanian. Instead Viola had lost nothing. She had only added. Doina’s Romanian, Assunta’s Neapolitan, Graziella’s Florentine, school Italian, even the English of video games. “It’s like one of our restorations,” said Giulia. “You don’t take anything away. You add layers. And in the end, if you do it well, you can see them all.”

Bellini, when he read the drafts of the article, told a memory of his own too. In 1972, in the third year of primary school, the teacher had set the essay “My dad”. He had written two pages about his taxi-driver father, the night fares, the smell of tobacco and petrol in the old white Fiat 600. But he had written “il mi’ babbo”, as he called him at home. The teacher had crossed out every “babbo” in red pen, writing “papà” above it, and had given him a four. Bellini had cried all afternoon. His father, that evening, had read the essay with the red corrections and said nothing. Then he had picked up the pen, crossed out every one of the teacher’s “papà” and written “babbo” back above them, in his crooked taxi driver’s handwriting. And underneath he had written: “Seen. Il babbo.” The next day the teacher had summoned the parents. His father hadn’t gone. “Now,” said Bellini, leafing through the drafts with a smile, “they’re putting that word in an archive at the National Library. My father would have been very proud. And the teacher, I hope, is turning in her grave.”

The article came out the following Sunday, across two full pages of the Gazzetta, with the title Bianca had chosen: “Icché tu dici? How Florence speaks today”. There were the interviews, the transcripts, a two-column table with Guido’s Florentine and Davide’s slang, a cartoon by Davide showing Guido and a boy in headphones talking with an interpreter in between, and a box titled “The words that are disappearing”, with Guido’s twenty words that nobody under fifty used any more. At the end of the article, Pietro and Bianca had written a conclusion Mancini liked very much. “There is no right Italian and wrong Italian,” they had written. “There are many Italians, each one right in its place. Guido’s is right in the workshop, Davide’s is right at the bar, Professor Orlandi’s is right in essays. Speaking well doesn’t mean always speaking the same way. It means knowing where you are and who you’re talking to. And now and then, when nobody can hear you, calling a friend ‘bischero’, with a smile.”

On Monday morning Professor Orlandi walked into class with the Gazzetta under her arm. She put it on her desk, open at the two pages of the article, and asked who had read it. Seven hands went up. Then she looked at Pietro, who went red to the ears, convinced he was about to get another lesson on register. Instead the teacher read the conclusion aloud, slowly, in the voice she used for Dante. When she got to “bischero”, she smiled, for the first time in three years. Then she told the class that this was exactly the point: writing well didn’t mean using big words, but choosing the right word for the right place. And that Pietro, in that article, had done exactly that. Then, in front of everyone, she took the register and changed the essay’s mark: from six and a half to seven. Not eight, she made clear, because the essay was still written in a tracksuit. But seven, because the article proved that Pietro knew perfectly well where he kept his good suit. The class applauded. Pietro, who had never been applauded at school, didn’t know where to look.

The article had a sequel nobody had foreseen. In the following days dozens of letters and messages arrived at the Gazzetta. A retired teacher from Prato sent a list of forty Prato words that were disappearing. A lady from San Frediano wrote that her grandmother said “sciocco” for bread without salt, and that after reading the article she had started saying it again, and her grandchildren made fun of her, but now they said it too. A group of students from a high school in Scandicci sent a ten-page dictionary of their slang, with definitions and examples, which Mancini decided to publish in instalments. And the City Council phoned to propose something that made Bianca jump out of her chair: to record the last speakers of broad Florentine, neighbourhood by neighbourhood, for a sound archive to be kept at the National Library, next to the books saved from the flood. They would start in January. The first interviewee, of course, would be Guido. Guido, when he heard, put on his Sunday suit to go to work in his shop, and didn’t take it off for three days.

There was another consequence too, smaller but enormous to Viola. Her teacher read the article and asked Guido whether he would like to come to class one Friday morning to teach the children the Florentine words of the old days. Guido accepted with an emotion he tried to hide behind a grumble. He turned up at the school in his Sunday suit, with a box of old shoes and a handwritten poster of twenty words, each with a drawing by Davide beside it: il cencio, la mezzina, l’uscio, il bischero. For an hour the children repeated the words in chorus, imitated the gorgia, laughed like mad at “la hoha hola hon la hannuccia”, and at the end Guido taught them all to say “gnamo” to go out into the playground. Viola, sitting in the front row with Assunta’s thimble on her thumb, was very proud. When a classmate asked her how she already knew all those words, she answered importantly: “Because I’m from the house.” That evening, at dinner, the teacher phoned Giulia to tell her that the children, leaving school, had all said goodbye with “gnamo”, and that two mothers had complained. Graziella, hearing this, slapped the table with both hands. “Then it works,” she said.

But Bianca made the most important recording on the last evening, almost by chance. She had stayed at the trattoria after closing to help clear the tables, and found Graziella in the kitchen, sitting on the stool, alone, leafing through the green notebook “Firenze parla” that Bianca had left on the table. Graziella was reading the list of disappearing words, one by one, moving her lips. At one point she stopped and said, without looking up: “Some are missing.” Bianca switched on the recorder, in silence. And for an hour Graziella dictated to her the words her mother Lucia used to say to her as a child, words she hadn’t spoken for fifty years. Kitchen words, mostly: “la mezzina”, the water jug; “il cencio”, the dishcloth; “la ramaiolata”, a ladleful of soup; “il pentolino”, “il tegamino”, “la teglia”. Household words: “l’uscio”, “la gruccia”, “il canterale”. Words of love: “il mi’ cittino”, my little one, which her mother said to her at night; “la mi’ bambina bella”. Then Graziella stopped. She said that Aldo, who was from Bologna, had learned all those words, one by one, to make her laugh. “He said ‘il mi’ cittino’ with a Bologna accent,” she said. “It was the funniest thing in the world.”

Bianca switched off the recorder only when Graziella had finished. They stayed silent for a moment, in the dark kitchen, with Aldo’s plant on the windowsill and the noise of the dishwasher. Then Graziella asked her what she would do with those words. Bianca said she would take them to the National Library archive in January, together with Guido’s. That they would stay there forever, with her voice, so that anyone, in a hundred years, could listen to them. Graziella nodded. Then she said something that Bianca transcribed that very night, at the top of the first page of the green notebook, before all the other words. “Words are like recipes,” said Graziella. “If nobody makes them any more, they disappear. Writing them down isn’t enough. You have to use them. A little every day. Like salt.” She stood up, switched off the light above the stove, and as she left the kitchen she turned to Bianca and said, with a smile Bianca had never seen on her before: “Goodnight, la mi’ bambina bella.” Bianca was left alone in the dark. And she understood that that word, at least, would not disappear.
